title: Mass & Energy Analysis of Control Volumes
source: Cengel, Boles & Kanoglu — Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Ch. 5
summary:
Now mass is allowed to flow across the boundary: we analyse a **control volume** (open system) — a turbine, nozzle, pump, pipe. Two balances govern it. The **mass balance**, $\dot m_{in} - \dot m_{out} = dm_{cv}/dt$, simply says mass is conserved. The **mass flow rate** through a cross-section is $\dot m = \rho V A = VA/v$, where $V$ is the average velocity, $A$ the area, $v$ the specific volume.

Flowing fluid carries energy in an extra way: to push a fluid element into the control volume the upstream fluid must do **flow work**, $w_{flow} = Pv$ per unit mass. Adding this to internal, kinetic and potential energy gives the energy a *flowing* stream transports — and $u + Pv$ is exactly enthalpy, so the natural carrier is $\theta = h + V^2/2 + gz$. This is why enthalpy, not internal energy, appears in every flow equation.

Most devices run at **steady state**: nothing in the control volume changes with time, so $dm_{cv}/dt = 0$ and $dE_{cv}/dt = 0$. Mass in equals mass out, and the **steady-flow energy equation (SFEE)** for a single stream becomes $\dot Q - \dot W = \dot m\big[(h_2 - h_1) + \tfrac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2} + g(z_2 - z_1)\big]$. Everything in the chapter is this one equation with terms switched off.

The art is knowing **which terms vanish for each device**. A **nozzle/diffuser** does no work and is ~adiabatic, trading enthalpy for kinetic energy: $h_1 + V_1^2/2 = h_2 + V_2^2/2$. A **turbine** or **compressor/pump** is adiabatic with negligible $\Delta KE,\Delta PE$, so $\dot W = \dot m(h_1 - h_2)$. A **throttling valve** has no work and no heat, giving the signature result $h_1 = h_2$ (enthalpy is preserved, temperature usually drops). **Heat exchangers** and **mixing chambers** apply the mass and energy balances across multiple streams.

The workflow mirrors Ch 4: write both balances, declare the steady-state and device assumptions, cancel the dead terms, and solve.

equations.name: Mass flow rate
equations.useWhen: Relating velocity, cross-sectional area, and flow rate at any inlet or outlet — e.g. sizing a pipe or finding exit velocity from a nozzle.
equations.note: $V$ = average velocity, $v$ = specific volume, $\dot V = VA$ = volume flow rate.

equations.name: Mass balance (steady)
equations.useWhen: Any steady-flow device. For one inlet and one outlet the mass flow is the same at both — the basis for nozzle/diffuser velocity changes.

equations.name: Flow work & flowing-fluid energy
equations.useWhen: Whenever a stream crosses the boundary. The flow-work term $Pv$ merges with $u$ into enthalpy $h$ — the reason $h$ appears in flow problems.
equations.note: This is why open systems use $h$ where closed systems used $u$.

equations.name: Steady-flow energy equation (single stream)
equations.latex: \dot Q - \dot W = \dot m\left[(h_2 - h_1) + \frac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2} + g(z_2 - z_1)\right]
equations.useWhen: The master equation for one-inlet/one-outlet steady devices. Cancel the terms that are zero for the specific device, then solve.
equations.note: Per unit mass, divide through by $\dot m$. Sign convention: $\dot Q$ in +, $\dot W$ out +.

equations.name: Nozzle / diffuser
equations.useWhen: A nozzle (speeds flow up) or diffuser (slows it down): no work, ~adiabatic, $\Delta pe \approx 0$. Enthalpy and kinetic energy trade off.
equations.note: Nozzle: $h$ drops, $V$ rises. Diffuser: the reverse.

equations.name: Turbine / compressor / pump
equations.useWhen: Adiabatic work devices with negligible $\Delta KE, \Delta PE$. Turbine: output work, $h$ drops. Compressor/pump: input work, $h$ rises.
equations.note: For a liquid pump, $\dot W_{pump} \approx \dot m\, v(P_2 - P_1)$ since $\Delta h \approx v\Delta P$.

equations.name: Throttling valve
equations.useWhen: Flow through a valve, capillary, or porous plug: no work, ~adiabatic, negligible $\Delta KE,\Delta PE$. The defining isenthalpic process.
equations.note: Pressure drops sharply; for most fluids temperature also drops (the basis of refrigeration).

equations.name: Heat exchanger / mixing chamber
rearrangements: \dot m_1 h_1 + \dot m_2 h_2 = \dot m_3 h_3 \ (\text{mixing})
equations.useWhen: Multiple streams exchange or combine energy with no external work and (for the whole device) no net heat loss. Combine with the mass balance.
equations.note: Choose the control volume so external $\dot Q$ and $\dot W$ vanish; then energy in = energy out.

glossary.definition: A region in space chosen for analysis, with mass and energy allowed to cross its boundary (control surface). An open system.
Mass passing a cross-section per unit time, $\dot m = \rho V A = VA/v$ (kg/s).
Volume passing per unit time, $\dot V = V A = \dot m\, v$ (m³/s).
Work needed to push unit mass across the boundary, $w_{flow} = Pv$. Combines with $u$ to form enthalpy.
Conditions at every point of the control volume stay constant in time: $dm_{cv}/dt = 0$ and $dE_{cv}/dt = 0$.
Energy balance for a steady control volume: $\dot Q - \dot W = \dot m[\Delta h + \Delta ke + \Delta pe]$.
Devices that change flow velocity with no work; enthalpy and kinetic energy trade off ($h_1 + V_1^2/2 = h_2 + V_2^2/2$).
Extracts shaft work from a flowing fluid as its enthalpy drops; $\dot W = \dot m(h_1 - h_2)$.
Adds energy to a fluid using input work, raising its pressure/enthalpy.
A flow restriction that drops pressure with no work or heat; isenthalpic, $h_1 = h_2$.
Transfers heat between two streams that don't mix; overall energy in = energy out.
Combines two or more streams into one; solved with mass and energy balances together.

tips: **Two balances, every time.** Write the mass balance *and* the energy balance. For mixing chambers and heat exchangers the mass balance supplies the relation you need to close the energy balance.

**Learn the device → cancellation map.** Nozzle/diffuser: $\dot W = 0$. Turbine/compressor: $\dot Q \approx 0$, $\Delta ke,\Delta pe \approx 0$. Throttle: $\dot W = \dot Q = 0$ → $h_1 = h_2$. This is the heart of the chapter.
**Enthalpy, not internal energy.** Flow work folds into $h$, so open-system equations carry $h$. Don't reach for $u$ in a steady-flow device.

**Only keep $\Delta KE$ when velocities are large** (nozzles, diffusers, high-speed jets). For turbines, pumps, heat exchangers it's usually negligible — but $\Delta KE$ is the *whole point* of a nozzle.
**Throttling is isenthalpic, not isothermal.** $h$ is constant; temperature generally changes (usually drops). Use the table to find the downstream state from $h_2 = h_1$.
**Pump shortcut for liquids:** $\dot W_{pump} \approx \dot m\,v(P_2 - P_1)$, because a liquid's specific volume barely changes.
